questions.qtext:
Consider the IP address $132.239.15.87.$

Suppose that we were still using class-based addressing and the network administrator had decided to break the network into $16$ different subnets of equal size, What is the subnet address of the subnet to which this IP address would be attached?
questions.solution:
Answer: B

Source solution 1 (score: 11)
132.239.15.87 => Class B
for 16 subnets, borrow 4 bits from the host portion of Class B
11111111.11111111.11110000.00000000 => 255.255.240.0

Subnet Address = IP AND MASK => 132.239.15.87 AND 255.255.240.0 => 132.239.0.0
Source solution 2 (score: 5)

For IP Address: 132.239.15.87,

Given that it is class-based addressing. Breaking down the IP address into binary, we get:

10000100.11101111.00001111.01010111

Since it starts with 10, it belongs to Class B. # of Network ID bits in Class B is, 16.

So we can say: 132.239.15.87/16.

  • Administrator had decided to break the network into 16 different subnets of equal size.

If we’re borrowing n host bits, then there will be 2^n subnets. From this, since we want 16 subnets of equal size, we need to borrow 4 host bits.

After borrowing 4 host bits we have, 132.239.15.87/20

132.239.00000000.00000000 to 132.239.00001111.11111111

The subnet address of the subnet to which this IP address would be attached is, 132.239.0.0

Hence, B is the answer.

A small university campus is assigned a large address block $12.1.0.0/17,$ but is only using a portion of these addresses $(\text{in}\; 12.1.1.0/24)$ to number its computers.

The university network is connected to interface $4$ of router $\text{R2,}$ Routing table of both routers are also given in the diagram.
Suppose the router $\mathrm{R} 1$ receives a packet with destination IP address $12.1.20.1.$ What path does this packet follow?
questions.solution:
Answer: B

Source solution 1 (score: 2)

Question: What path does a packet with destination 12.1.20.1 follow?

Analysis:

  1. Packet Arrives at R1:

    • Destination IP: 12.1.20.1

    • R1 Routing Table:

      • Entry 1: 12.1.0.0/17 -> Interface 2 (to R2)

      • Entry 2: 0.0.0.0/0 -> Interface 1 (Internet)

    • Matching:

      • Does 12.1.20.1 match 12.1.0.0/17?

      • /17 means the first 17 bits must match.

      • 12.1 matches 12.1 (first 16 bits).

      • 17th bit check:

        • Network: 12.1.0.0 (3rd octet 0 = 00000000).

        • Dest: 12.1.20.1 (3rd octet 20 = 00010100).

        • The 17th bit (first bit of 3rd octet) is 0 for both. Match!

    • Decision: R1 forwards packet to Interface 2 (towards R2).

  2. Packet Arrives at R2:

    • Destination IP: 12.1.20.1

    • R2 Routing Table:

      • Entry 1: 12.1.1.0/24 -> Interface 4 (Internal Network)

      • Entry 2: 0.0.0.0/0 -> Interface 3 (Default, back to R1)

    • Matching:

      • Does 12.1.20.1 match 12.1.1.0/24?

      • Prefix check: 12.1.1 vs 12.1.20.

      • The third octet (1 vs 20) is different. No Match.

    • Decision: No specific match found. R2 uses the Default Route (0.0.0.0/0).

    • The Default Route points to Interface 3 (back to R1).

  3. Packet Arrives Back at R1:

    • R1 receives the packet again.

    • R1 checks table -> Matches 12.1.0.0/17 -> Sends to R2.

    • R2 checks table -> No match -> Default Route -> Sends to R1.

Conclusion: The packet bounces back and forth between R1 and R2 in a routing loop until the TTL (Time-To-Live) expires.

Sequence: 1→2 (R1 sends to R2) 3→2 (R2 sends back to R1 via Int 3... wait, let's look at the diagram interfaces).

  • R1 is connected to R2 via link 2-3.

  • Path: R1 receives (from 1), sends out 2.

  • R2 receives on 3.

  • R2 sends out... default route says "Interface 3".

  • So R2 sends it right back out Interface 3.

  • R1 receives on Interface 2.

  • R1 sends out Interface 2.

Path: 1→2→3→2→3→2…

Answer: B. 1→2→3→2→3→2→3…

Source solution 2 (score: 1)
$12.1.20.1$ on Router $R1$ till $17$ bits are matching so Router will forward it to port $2$ now Router $2$ will send it port $3$ as $24$ bits are not matching now again it comes to $R1$ and $R1$ will do the same as it does previously so ultimately it will be infinite so $B$ should be the ans .
Source solution 3 (score: 0)
B
Source solution 4 (score: 0)
Option A: INCORRECT becoz given destination add will not match with port 4 as it will never give 12.1.20.1 becoz port 4 has first 24 bits fixed

Option B: CORRECT becoz the pkt will start from port 1 and will move to port 2 becoz first 17 bits are matching then it will move to port 3 of R2.Further from port 3 it will come back to port 2 due to longest prefix match and from 2 it will again move to port 3 and will continue like this infinetely

Option C: INCORRECT becoz from port 2 it will move further towards port 3 due to longest prefix match

Option D: INCORRECT becoz from port 2 it will move further towards port 3 due to longest prefix match and will not move back to port 1 (could have moved back to port 1 if port 3 had not matched)

Pretend for a moment that IP addresses are $12$ bits instead of $32,$ and suppose you are allocated the block of addresses $\textsf{1011xxxxxxx}$ (i.e., all addresses that start with '$1011$' in binary notation). The network administrator has divided this network into $4$ subnets as follows:

  • Network $\text{A}$ uses prefix $/ 5$
  • Network $\text{B}$ uses prefix /6
  • Network $\text{C}$ uses prefix $/ 7$
  • Network $\text{D}$ uses prefix $/ 8$

After the subnetting, which of the following is true?

options.text: There is only one unused block left of size $2^3$
There is only one unused block left of size $2^4$
There is only one unused block left of size $2^ 5$
There is only one unused block left of size $2^ 6$

questions.solution:
Answer: B

Source solution 1 (score: 5)

Number of IP addresses of $8$-bit (as all addresses start with ‘$1011$’ which is fixed) = $2^8 = 256$

  • Network $A$ uses prefix $/5$

$\text{No. of IP addresses} = 2^{(12-5)} = 2^7 = 128$

  • Network $B$ uses prefix $/6$

$\text{No. of IP addresses} = 2^{(12-6)} = 2^6 = 64$

  • Network $B$ uses prefix $/7$

$\text{No. of IP addresses} = 2^{(12-7)} = 2^5 = 32$

  • Network $B$ uses prefix $/8$

$\text{No. of IP addresses} = 2^{(12-8)} = 2^4 = 16$

$\therefore$ $\text{Unused block} = 256-(128+64+32+16) = 16 = 2^4$

$\color{Green} Ans: B$

Source solution 2 (score: 2)

Total number of IP addresses possible from 8 bits (bcoz 4 are fixed): 2^8 = 256

Number of IP addresses used by
Network A: 2^(12 - 5) = 2^7 = 128
Network B: 2^6 - 2 = 2^(12 - 6) = 2^6 = 64
Network C: 2^7 - 2 = 2^(12 - 7) = 2^5 = 32
Network D: 2^8 - 2 = 2^(12 - 8) = 2^4 = 16

Total unused => 256-(128+64+32+16)=256-240=16 => 2^4 => B

Source solution 3 (score: 2)

Consider the forwarding table of some router $\mathrm{R}$ as follows -
$$ \begin{array}{lcl} \qquad \qquad \textbf{Prefix } & & \textbf{Outgoing Interface} \\ \hline \texttt{11010110 01100001 11111111 11000000} & & \text{Port b} \\ \texttt{11010110 01100001 11111111 10000000} & & \text{Port c} \\ \texttt{11010110 01100001 11111111 00000000} & & \text{Port b} \\ \texttt{11010110 01100001 11111110 00000000} & & \text{Port a} \end{array} $$
Suppose we perform route aggregation on the table (such that routing decisions are unchanged for incoming IP packets to $\text{R})$ then what will be the number of rows after aggregation?
questions.solution:
Answer: 4

Selected solution (score: 12)

We can aggregate only those having same outgoing interface but here if we aggregate them routing decisions will be changed. So we won’t aggregate them.

Suppose we aggregate them ⇒

\[ {\color{green}{11010110\;01100001\;11111111}}\;{\color{red}{000000}} \] or \[ {\color{green}{11010110\;01100001\;11111111}}\;{\color{red}{0}} \quad(\text{Don’t know}) \]

Now suppose

\[ {\color{green}{11010110\;01100001\;11111111}}\;{\color{red}{1111}} \]

arrives at router, initially it would have gone to Port B by longest match with first entry.

After aggregating it will have its longest match with the 2nd entry and forward to Port C.

Before Aggregating :

\[ \begin{aligned} {\color{green}{11010110\;01100001\;11111111}}\;{\color{red}{110000}} &\quad \text{Port B (longer match)} \\[6pt] {\color{green}{11010110\;01100001\;11111111}}\;{\color{red}{111}} \\[14pt] {\color{green}{11010110\;01100001\;11111111}}\;{\color{red}{1}} &\quad \text{Port C} \\[6pt] {\color{green}{11010110\;01100001\;11111111}}\;{\color{red}{1111}} \end{aligned} \]

After Aggregating :

\[ \begin{aligned} {\color{green}{11010110\;01100001\;11111111}}\;{\color{red}{000000}} &\quad \text{Port B} \\[6pt] {\color{green}{11010110\;01100001\;11111111}}\;{\color{red}{111}} \\[14pt] {\color{green}{11010110\;01100001\;11111111}}\;{\color{red}{1}} &\quad \text{Port C (Longer Match)} \\[6pt] {\color{green}{11010110\;01100001\;11111111}}\;{\color{red}{1111}} \end{aligned} \]
Source solution 2 (score: 4)

In such types of aggregation questions, always keep in mind to check if any routing decision has changed or not.
If yes, then don't do that aggregation.

Source solution 3 (score: 3)

We can reduce the number of entries by grouping the longest prefix matches for the same outgoing interface. This creates new entries where the first column is the longest common prefix between them, and the second column is their outgoing port.

However, we must ensure that such grouping does not create conflicts with other interfaces.

In the given forwarding table, multiple entries correspond to Port B. At first glance, it may seem possible to combine them into a single entry using their common prefix. But before doing so, we must verify whether such aggregation affects how packets are routed.

Possible aggregation could be:

$\texttt{11010110 01100001 11111111 11000000}$
$\texttt{11010110 01100001 11111111 00000000}$

Now suppose an incoming IP packet
$\texttt{11010110 01100001 11111111 111111}$
arrives at the router.

Before Aggregation
11010110 01100001 11111111 110000 → Port B
11010110 01100001 11111111 1 → Port C

The router performs a longest prefix match on the incoming address. Here, the packet 11010110 01100001 11111111 111111 matches the first entry more closely (longer prefix) and is therefore forwarded to Port B.

After Aggregation
11010110 01100001 11111111 000000 → Port B
11010110 01100001 11111111 1 → Port C

Now, after aggregation, the same packet 11010110 01100001 11111111 111111 finds its longest prefix match with the second entry instead of the first, and is therefore forwarded to Port C.

This shows that aggregation changes the forwarding behavior of the router.

🎥 Detailed Video Solution by DVRUO Classes
Source solution 4 (score: 0)

This is the correct approach. Let's solve it again using Strict Aggregation rules, calculating the specific ranges to prove why they cannot be merged.

1. Calculate the Ranges

First, let's look at the full address space provided in the table. We will focus on the 3rd Octet (which distinguishes Row 4) and the 4th Octet (which distinguishes Rows 1, 2, 3).

  • Prefix P: 11010110 01100001 (Common to all). Let's ignore this for clarity and look at the changing parts.

Row3rd Octet4th Octet PrefixCIDR NotationDecimal Range (3rd.4th)Interface
411111110 (254)00000000...254.0/24254.0 to 254.255Port a
311111111 (255)0......255.0/25255.0 to 255.127Port b
211111111 (255)10......255.128/26255.128 to 255.191Port c
111111111 (255)11......255.192/26255.192 to 255.255Port b

2. Visualize the "Number Line"

Strict aggregation requires that blocks be contiguous (touching each other) AND share the same interface.

Let's look at the timeline of addresses for the 255.x network:

  • Range 1 (0 - 127): Goes to Port b.

  • Range 2 (128 - 191): Goes to Port c.

  • Range 3 (192 - 255): Goes to Port b.

3. Why Strict Aggregation Fails

To reduce the number of rows, we look for opportunities to merge.

Attempt 1: Merge Port b (Row 3 and Row 1)

  • Row 3 ends at .127.

  • Row 1 starts at .192.

  • The Gap: There is a gap between .127 and .192. This gap is occupied by Row 2 (Port c).

  • Rule Violation: Because the address space for Port b is discontiguous (interrupted by Port c), you cannot merge them into a single strict aggregate. You cannot draw a box around the "Port b" addresses without accidentally capturing the "Port c" addresses inside it.

Attempt 2: Merge Port a (Row 4) with Port b

  • Row 4 is 254.x.

  • Row 3 is 255.x.

  • Contiguity: They are numerically adjacent (254 ends where 255 begins).

  • Rule Violation: They go to different interfaces (Port a vs Port b). Therefore, they cannot be aggregated.

4. Final Conclusion

Since no two rows satisfy both conditions (Same Interface + Contiguous Range), NO aggregation is possible under strict rules.

You must keep every single entry:

  1. ...254.0/24 (Port a)

  2. ...255.0/25 (Port b)

  3. ...255.128/26 (Port c)

  4. ...255.192/26 (Port b)

Final Answer: 4 Rows.

Source solution 5 (score: 0)
Answer

4

Explanation

The key is that these are CIDR prefixes of different lengths, inferred from the trailing zeroes.

Binary prefixCIDR prefixPort
11010110 01100001 11111111 11000000216.97.255.192/26b
11010110 01100001 11111111 10000000216.97.255.128/25c
11010110 01100001 11111111 00000000216.97.255.0/24b
11010110 01100001 11111110 00000000216.97.254.0/23a


Remember that routers use Longest Prefix Match (LPM).

Step 1: Which traffic goes where?

The /23 route covers:

  • 216.97.254.0 – 216.97.255.255 → Port a

Then the more specific entries override parts of it.

So the final forwarding is:

  • 216.97.254.* → Port a

  • 216.97.255.0 – 216.97.255.127 → Port b (because of /24)

  • 216.97.255.128 – 216.97.255.191 → Port c (because of /25)

  • 216.97.255.192 – 216.97.255.255 → Port b (because of /26)

Step 2: Can any entries be merged?

Aggregation is only possible if:

  • the resulting prefix is valid,

  • it sends packets to the same interface, and

  • routing decisions remain unchanged.

Let's check.

Can /24 and /26 be merged?

No. The addresses between 216.97.255.128–191 must still go to Port c.

If you tried to replace them with one larger prefix, that range would also be sent to Port b, changing the routing.

Can /25 and /26 be merged?

No. They go to different ports (c and b).

Can /23 and /24 be merged?

No. They go to different ports (a and b).

Therefore:

None of the four entries is redundant, and no two entries can be combined without changing the forwarding behavior.

So after aggregation, the routing table is unchanged.

$$\boxed{\text{Number of rows}=4}$$

A Quick Visualization
216.97.254.* -> a (/23)
216.97.255.0 - 127 -> b (/24)
216.97.255.128 - 191 -> c (/25)
216.97.255.192 - 255 -> b (/26)

Notice that the b → c → b pattern inside the 216.97.255.* block prevents any aggregation. If the last /26 had also gone to Port c, then aggregation would have been possible.

questions.solution:
Answer: D

Selected solution (score: 1)
$\underbrace{128}_{8-bit}.\underbrace{8}_{8-bit}.\underbrace{16}_{8-bit}.\underbrace{0}_{8-bit}/20$

$\text{First Address:}\; 128.8.16.0/{\color{SkyBlue}20} \;\;\;\; 10000000\;\;00001000\;\;0001{\color{SkyBlue}0000}\;\;{\color{SkyBlue}00000000}\;\; \equiv 128.8.16.0$

$\text{Last Address:}\;\; 128.8.16.0/{\color{SkyBlue}20} \;\;\;\; 10000000\;\;00001000\;\;0001{\color{SkyBlue}1111}\;\;{\color{SkyBlue}11111111}\;\; \equiv 128.8.31.255$

$\therefore$ The address range is: $128.8.16.0-128.8.31.255$

Task: Aggregate the routing table rows without changing routing decisions and determine the number of rows remaining.

Analysis:

  1. Current Table:

    • 128.2.0.0/24 $\rightarrow$ Interface 1

    • 128.2.1.0/24 $\rightarrow$ Interface 2

    • 128.2.2.0/24 $\rightarrow$ Interface 2

    • 128.2.3.0/24 $\rightarrow$ Interface 3

  2. Aggregation Strategy (Longest Prefix Match):

    We look for a way to group these subnets into a larger "supernet" while preserving the correct destination for each specific subnet.

    • Notice that the subnets 0.0, 1.0, 2.0, and 3.0 are contiguous. Together, they form the block 128.2.0.0/22 (which covers 128.2.0.0 to 128.2.3.255).

    • Interfaces 2 handles two of these subnets (1.0 and 2.0). This is the "majority" interface.

    • We can create a broad rule for the whole /22 block pointing to Interface 2, and then create specific "exceptions" (longer prefixes) for the subnets that don't go to Interface 2.

  3. New Optimized Table:

    • Row 1 (General Rule): 128.2.0.0/22 $\rightarrow$ Interface 2

      (This covers 0.0, 1.0, 2.0, and 3.0)

    • Row 2 (Exception for Int 1): 128.2.0.0/24 $\rightarrow$ Interface 1

      (Because /24 is longer than /22, packets for 0.0 will match this row and go to Int 1 correctly.)

    • Row 3 (Exception for Int 3): 128.2.3.0/24 $\rightarrow$ Interface 3

      (Packets for 3.0 will match this longer prefix and go to Int 3 correctly.)

  4. Verification:

    • Packet to 128.2.1.x: Matches Row 1 only. Goes to Interface 2. (Correct)

    • Packet to 128.2.2.x: Matches Row 1 only. Goes to Interface 2. (Correct)

    • This setup uses 3 rows. It is impossible to reduce it to 2 rows because we have 3 distinct interfaces that must be reachable.

Answer: The number of rows after aggregation is 3.

questions.qtext:
Consider two subnets connected to $\text{R1}$ as shown below.

The interface IPs are also shown in the given diagram.

Please note that for every subnet all-zeros address is reserved for the network name, and the all-ones address is reserved for broadcast. The network administrator wants to set up subnet masks so that the network prefix has maximal length.

What should be maximal length subnet masks for both subnets?
questions.solution:
Answer: B

Source solution 1 (score: 14)

In $Subnet\ 1$ IP address of host $H1$ is $128.100.11.2$ and interface IP address is $128.100.11.70$
$\ \ 2 = (0000\ 0010)_2$
$70 = (0100\ 0110)_2$

For network id take all the bits from first $3$ octets, and from the $3rd$ octet take first bit as these bits are the same in both.
Hence, the maximal length of the $Subnet\ 1$ is $/25$.


In $Subnet\ 2$ IP address of host $H2$ is $128.100.10.14$ and interface IP address is $128.100.10.15$
$14 = (0000\ 1110)_2$
$15 = (0000\ 1111)_2$

For network id take all the bits from first $3$ octets.
Now here comes the tricky part and the beauty of this question!
How many bits form the $3rd$ octet should we take for network id? $\Longrightarrow$ $7\ bits$ means the net mask is $/31$ right ?
No, netmask can't be $/31$ as in this network only $2$ IPs are possible $128.100.10.14$ and $128.100.10.15$ but we need these IPs for $Subnet\_id$ and $DBA$.

So, should we take $/30$ ? $\Longrightarrow$ again $NO$

Because in $/30$ the last IP is $128.100.10.15$, which we need for $DBA$, hence can't assign this to interface. For the same reason the netmask can't be $/29,\ /28$.

Hence, the maximal length of the $Subnet\ 2$ is $/27$ with IP range of $128.100.10.0\ \text{to}\ 128.100.10.31$

$\text{Correct Answer:}\ B$

Watch this: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=k3ZhUbeCyNA&t=1776s

Source solution 2 (score: 1)

Task: Determine the subnet masks for Subnet 1 and Subnet 2.

Analysis:

  1. Subnet 1: Contains IPs 128.100.11.2 and 128.100.11.70.

    • Binary of last octet:

      • 2 = 00000010

      • 70 = 01000110

    • They differ at the 2nd bit (value 64). Therefore, the subnet mask cannot match up to that bit. It can match only the first bit (0).

    • This implies a $/25$ mask (matches first 25 bits). A $/26$ would split them into different subnets (0-63 and 64-127).

  2. Subnet 2: Contains IPs 128.100.10.15 and 128.100.10.14.

    • Binary of last octet:

      • 14 = 00001110

      • 15 = 00001111

    • Constraint: "All-zeros is network, all-ones is broadcast". This means a host IP cannot be the broadcast address.

    • Let's check mask sizes for a block starting at .0:

      • /28 (Block size 16): Range is 0 to 15. Broadcast is 15. Since 15 is used as an IP address, this mask is invalid.

      • /27 (Block size 32): Range is 0 to 31. Broadcast is 31. 15 is a valid host address. This works.

    • Therefore, the maximal length mask is /27.

  3. Conclusion: Subnet 1 is $/25$, Subnet 2 is $/27$.

Answer: The correct option is B.

Source solution 3 (score: 0)

Subnet 1:

We look directly at where the bits of the two IP addresses match in the last octet.

  • R1: 128.100.11. 0 1 0 0 0 1 1 0 (70)
  • H1: 128.100.11. 0 0 0 0 0 0 1 0 (2)

Let's check the prefix lengths by counting from left to right in the last octet:

  • 1st bit: Both start with 0. (Valid for /25)
  • 2nd bit: R1 has 1, but H1 has 0. (Fails for /26)
    Because the 2nd bit is different, any network prefix longer than /25 splits them into different networks.

Maximal prefix length = 24 + 1 = /25

Subnet 2: Checking Host ID Bits

Both IPs share the prefix 128.100.10.000011__. Let's test masks by changing the remaining host ID bits.
king method.

Checking /31 Mask (1 Host Bit)
  • Template: 128.100.10. 0000 111 _

Under a /31 prefix length, there is only 1 bit left for the Host ID (the very last bit). Let's list the possibilities for that 1 bit:

\begin{array}{c|c|l} \textbf{Host ID Bit} & \textbf{Last Octet Value} & \textbf{Role} \\ \hline 0 & 14 & \textbf{Network ID (All Zeros) } \mathbf{\times} \\ 1 & 15 & \textbf{Broadcast ID (All Ones) } \mathbf{\times} \\ \end{array}

❌ Failed:

  • 14 becomes the Network ID (because its host bit is 0). Therefore, it cannot be assigned to host H2.
  • 15 becomes the Broadcast ID (because its host bit is 1). Therefore, it cannot be assigned to R1.

With a /31 mask, there are 0 usable host addresses left in this block.

Checking /30 Mask (2 Host Bits)
  • Template: 128.100.10. 0000 11 _ _

\begin{array}{c|c|l} \textbf{Host ID Bits} & \textbf{Last Octet Value} & \textbf{Role} \\ \hline 00 & 12 & \text{Network ID (All Zeros)} \\ 01 & 13 & \text{Usable Host} \\ 10 & 14 & \text{Usable Host (H2)} \\ 11 & 15 & \textbf{Broadcast ID (All Ones) } \mathbf{\times} \\ \end{array}

❌ Failed: 15 is the Broadcast ID. It cannot be assigned to R1.

Checking /29 Mask (3 Host Bits)
  • Template: 128.100.10. 0000 1 _ _ _

Task: Identify the true statements.

Analysis:

  • A. False. You cannot always aggregate routes. If contiguous routes point to different next-hop routers, aggregating them would send traffic for both to a single router, breaking connectivity for one.

  • B. True. Packet to 31.75.93.129.

    • Matches 31.75/16? Yes.

    • Matches 31.75.93.128/25? Yes (129 is in range 128-255).

    • Longest Prefix Match chooses the /25 route $\rightarrow$ port 2.

  • C. True. A routing table can contain nested prefixes (e.g., a /17 and a /18 with the same base address). This is a standard feature of CIDR used to create routing exceptions (sending a specific sub-block to a different path than the main block).

  • D. True. This describes a valid algorithm for Longest Prefix Match. If you scan prefixes sorted by length (shortest to longest), the last one that matches will naturally be the longest one.

Answer: Statements B, C, and D are true.

Consider three routers $\text{R1, R2, and R3}$ connected as follows


As shown in the diagram, $\text{R1}$ is connected to the subnet with the subnet id as $24.4.6.0,$ also $\text{R2}$ is connected to the subnet with the subnet id as $24.4.6.128.$

The netmask used in the network is $/26.$

What are the possible combinations of IP addresses of given interfaces $a,b,x,y,c,$ and $d?$

Consider each option as an independent option.
questions.solution:
Answer: B

Source solution 1 (score: 5)

This question is much easier than it looks:

Just remember that each distinct interface from the router represents a separate network(or subnet). read=text read

  • $a$ and $24.4.6.0/26$ on same subnet
  • $c$ and $24.4.6.128/26$ on same subnet
  • $b$ and $x$ must be on the same subnet.
  • $y$ and $d$ must be on the same subnet
  • $a$ and $b$ must be on different subnets
  • $c$ and $d$ must be on different subnets
  • $x$ and $y$ must be on different subnets
  • $b$ and $y$ must be on different subnets
  • $b$ and $d$ must be on different subnets
  • $x$ and $d$ must be on different subnets

Following all the above rules,

OPTIONSANALYSISRESULT
Ax and y are on the same subnetELIMINATED
BAll rules satisfiedACCEPTED
Cx and d are on the same subnetELIMINATED
Db and y are on the same subnetELIMINATED

Source solution 2 (score: 2)

The correct answer is B.

⏱️ The 30-Second Exam Rules

To solve this type of question rapidly in an exam, look for two fundamental networking rules:

  1. The Link Rule: Interfaces on the same physical cable/link (like $b$ and $x$, or $y$ and $d$) must belong to the exact same subnet block.
  2. The Router Rule: A single router (like $R$) cannot have two interfaces (like $x$ and $y$) inside the same subnet block.
Step-by-Step Shortcut

First, break down the IP address ranges using the /26 netmask (block size of 64):

  • Subnet 0: .0 to .63 (Contains a)
  • Subnet 1: .64 to .127
  • Subnet 2: .128 to .191 (Contains c)
  • Subnet 3: .192 to .255
Speed Elimination of Options:
  • Option A: $x = .250$ and $y = .200$. Both are in Subnet 3. Router $R$ cannot have two interfaces on the same subnet. ❌ (Violates Router Rule)
  • Option C: $x = .195$ and $y = .250$. Both are in Subnet 3. Router $R$ cannot have two interfaces on the same subnet. ❌ (Violates Router Rule)
  • Option D: $b = .195$ (Subnet 3) and $y = .200$ (Subnet 3) with $d = .250$ (Subnet 3). This forces both links on either side of Router $R$ into Subnet 3, making $R$'s interfaces $x$ and $y$ occupy the same subnet. ❌ (Violates Router Rule)
Why Option B is Perfectly Valid:
  • $a = .1$ $\rightarrow$ Belongs to Subnet 0 (Valid)
  • $b = .195$ and $x = .200$ $\rightarrow$ Both belong to Subnet 3 (Valid link)
  • $y = .68$ $\rightarrow$ Belongs to Subnet 1 (Valid, since Router $R$ now correctly has $x$ in Subnet 3 and $y$ in Subnet 1)

Source solution 3 (score: 1)

Task: Find the valid combination of IP addresses for interfaces $a, b, x, y, c, d$.

Analysis:

  1. Subnet Constraints:

    • Left LAN ($R1-a$): Connected to 24.4.6.0/26. Range: .0 to .63.

    • Right LAN ($R2-c$): Connected to 24.4.6.128/26. Range: .128 to .191.

    • Available Space: The total network seems to be a /24. The unused blocks are .64 - .127 (/26) and .192 - .255 (/26).

  2. Link Constraints:

    • The link between $R1 (b)$ and $R (x)$ must be in the same subnet.

    • The link between $R (y)$ and $R2 (d)$ must be in the same subnet.

    • Crucially, since there is a router ($R$) between them, the link $b-x$ and the link $y-d$ must be in different subnets.

  3. Evaluating Option B:

    • $a: 24.4.6.1$ $\rightarrow$ Valid (in range 0-63).

    • $b: 24.4.6.195$ & $x: 24.4.6.200$ $\rightarrow$ Both are in the range 192-255. This places the first link in the upper available /26 subnet. This is valid.

    • $y: 24.4.6.68$ $\rightarrow$ This is in the range 64-127. This places the second link interface in the lower available /26 subnet.

    • Since the two router-to-router links use different, non-overlapping subnets, this configuration is valid.

Answer: The correct option is B.
